title: Talking Through Complexity
summary: Deriving and stating time/space complexity live and correctly — including amortized and multi-variable cases — instead of quoting a memorized answer.

slides.markdown:
"What's the complexity?" is the most predictable question in any coding round, and the most common miss isn't getting the answer wrong — it's giving an answer that doesn't match the code actually on the screen.

This topic is about **deriving** complexity live from the code you just wrote, not reciting a memorized number: naming multiple variables when there are two inputs, handling amortized costs without hand-waving, accounting for the call stack, and responding cleanly when the interviewer asks "can you do better?"

For what the notation formally means, see `data-structures-algorithms`'s complexity group — this topic is entirely about the live, spoken version of that skill.

slides.sectionTitle: Deriving from the code, not from memory
slides.markdown:
The habit that separates a correct answer from a *convincing* one: point at the actual loops and recursive calls in front of you and count from there, out loud. "This outer loop runs n times, and for each iteration this inner lookup is O(1) because it's a hash map access, so the total is O(n)."

Quoting a complexity you memorized for "this kind of problem" without re-deriving it against the code you actually wrote is how mismatches happen — you added an extra nested loop for an edge case halfway through and forgot to fold it back into the number you're about to state. Re-derive every time, even when you're confident you already know the answer.

slides.subTitle: O(V+E), O(n·m)
slides.markdown:
Many real problems have more than one size variable, and collapsing them into a single n hides information. Graph problems are the classic case: BFS/DFS is **O(V + E)**, not O(n²) — calling it O(n²) obscures that a sparse graph (E close to V) runs nearly linear, while a dense graph (E close to V²) does not.

Two strings of different lengths is another common case: comparing every character of one against every character of the other is **O(a·b)**, not O(n²) — writing n² implies the two inputs are the same size, which may not be true and can mislead about how the cost actually scales if only one grows.

Name every independent size variable before you start counting. "Let V be nodes, E be edges" takes five seconds and prevents the rest of the analysis from being ambiguous.

Dynamic array append is the cleanest example: each individual append is either O(1) — just write to the next slot — or occasionally O(n) when the array resizes and every existing element gets copied. Quoting either number alone is misleading.

The honest statement: "append is amortized O(1) — most calls are O(1), and the O(n) resizes happen exponentially less often as the array grows, so averaged over any sequence of appends, the cost per append is constant." That's a complete answer. Saying just "O(1)" glosses over the resize; saying just "O(n) worst case" overstates the typical cost. Amortized analysis exists precisely to give a fair single number for exactly this kind of lumpy cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Space complexity and the call stack
slides.markdown:
Space complexity gets stated less often than time, and when it is stated, the recursion stack is the part most commonly forgotten. A recursive solution with no explicit array or hash map can still be O(n) space, because each recursive call holds a stack frame until it returns — a naive recursive Fibonacci or a depth-first tree traversal on a skewed tree both pay this cost.

A complete space statement names both: "O(1) auxiliary beyond the input, but O(n) for the recursion stack in the worst case of a completely unbalanced tree." Converting the same logic to an iterative version with an explicit stack doesn't remove this cost — it just makes it visible in your own data structure instead of the call stack, which is worth saying if the interviewer asks how you'd reduce space.

slides.sectionTitle: Your solution vs the theoretical optimum
slides.markdown:
| | Your solution | Theoretical optimum |
|---|---|---|
| Comparison-based sort | O(n log n) | Ω(n log n) — provably can't do better with comparisons |
| Search in unsorted array | O(n) | Ω(n) — must be prepared to inspect every element |
| Search in sorted array | O(log n) | Ω(log n) — matches, this is optimal |
| Naive matrix multiply | O(n³) | roughly O(n^2.37) known, gap still open |

Stating where your solution sits relative to the known lower bound is a senior-level habit: "this is O(n log n), which is also the proven lower bound for comparison-based sorting, so there's no faster general algorithm without changing the model" reads very differently from silently stopping at your own answer without knowing whether better is even possible.

slides.sectionTitle: Quoting a complexity the code doesn't match
slides.markdown:
The most damaging complexity mistake isn't a wrong theoretical answer — it's a **mismatch between the stated complexity and the code on the screen**, because it signals you're reciting rather than analyzing.

This happens most often after a mid-solution edit: you added a `.sort()` call to fix a bug, or nested a lookup inside a loop to handle an edge case, and then state the complexity you had *before* that change. An interviewer who's tracking your code closely will catch this immediately, and it reads worse than simply not knowing — it suggests the complexity claim was never actually derived from the code at all.

The fix is mechanical: re-scan your actual code for its complexity right before you state it, every time, especially after any edit.

This question is asked constantly, sometimes even when the current answer is already optimal — it's a probe for how you reason under pressure, not necessarily a hint that a better solution exists.

A strong response has three possible honest shapes: "yes, here's the specific inefficiency I'd remove and how" (if you spot one), "I don't see an obvious way without changing the problem's constraints" (if you genuinely believe it's optimal — and ideally naming why, per §6), or "let me think about where the redundant work is" followed by actually looking, rather than a reflexive guess. What reads badly is either freezing, or inventing a fake optimization that doesn't actually reduce complexity just to have something to say.

Putting the whole topic together, a complete answer has four parts said together, in about fifteen seconds:

1. **Name every variable.** "n is the array length, k is the target count."
2. **State the tight bound and which case.** "Worst case O(n log k), from a heap of size k."
3. **State space separately, including the call stack if recursive.** "O(k) auxiliary for the heap."
4. **Note the practical caveat, if there is one.** "If k is close to n, I'd just sort instead and skip the heap overhead."

Most candidates give one of these four. Giving all four, unprompted, is what reads as fluency rather than a memorized fact.

This topic pairs directly with [narrating your approach](narrating-your-approach) — stating complexity is one specific, recurring beat inside that larger narration loop, not a separate ritual saved for the end.

For a much larger drill set specifically on complexity trade-off phrasing across many worked solutions, see `data-structures-algorithms`'s [complexity-tradeoff-communication](complexity-tradeoff-communication) topic; and for the underlying notation this topic assumes you already know, see that area's `complexity` group.
